nodes.label: MealMind
nodes.rationale: Positioned as an AI-powered recipe recommendation system that goes beyond text search by combining computer vision (ingredient detection from a camera) with generative AI (recipe images and cooking videos); the stated value is turning what a user physically has on hand into an actionable, media-rich recipe.

nodes.label: Smart Recipe Recommendations
nodes.rationale: Recipes are suggested from the set of ingredients the user actually has, rather than from free-text queries, so the recommender is constrained by real pantry state.

nodes.label: Ingredient Detection (camera-based)
nodes.rationale: Real-time object detection is chosen over manual ingredient entry to remove data-entry friction; this is why camera access is listed as a hard prerequisite.

nodes.label: Recipe Video Generation
nodes.rationale: Cooking tutorial videos are generated on demand via Google Flow instead of curated/licensed video, trading determinism and cost for unlimited per-recipe coverage.

nodes.label: Recipe Image Generation
nodes.rationale: Recipe photography is synthesized with Nano-Banana rather than sourced from a stock library, so every generated or long-tail recipe still gets a plated image.

nodes.label: Dietary Management
nodes.rationale: Dietary preferences and restrictions act as a filter layer over recommendations, which implies the recommender must be constraint-aware rather than purely similarity-driven.

nodes.label: Shopping List Generation
nodes.rationale: Closes the loop opposite to ingredient detection: detection tells the system what the user has, the shopping list derives what is missing for a chosen recipe.

nodes.label: ML Recommender System
nodes.rationale: Machine-learning based rather than rule-based matching, with trained models kept out of the app tree under ml_models/recommender_system so training and serving artifacts are versioned separately from application code.

nodes.label: Layered Backend Architecture (routes / services / models / schemas)
nodes.rationale: The backend is split into routes/ (HTTP surface), services/ (business logic and third-party AI integrations), models/ (SQLAlchemy persistence), schemas/ (Pydantic validation) and utils/. Each external AI provider is isolated behind a single service module so the route layer never touches a vendor SDK directly, which keeps provider swaps (Google Flow, Nano-Banana) local to one file.
nodes.norm_label: layered backend architecture (routes / services / models / schemas)

nodes.label: FastAPI
nodes.rationale: Chosen as a modern async web framework; the README leans on its built-in OpenAPI docs endpoint (/docs) as the API documentation surface, avoiding a separately maintained API spec.

nodes.label: Uvicorn / Gunicorn ASGI serving
nodes.rationale: Development runs bare uvicorn with --reload; production runs gunicorn with 4 UvicornWorker processes to get process-level parallelism and supervision that a single uvicorn process does not provide.

nodes.label: Alembic Migrations
nodes.rationale: A single migration chain (alembic upgrade head) is used for both SQLite dev and PostgreSQL prod, with the target selected only by DATABASE_URL in .env, so schema drift between environments is avoided.

nodes.label: Dual Database Strategy (SQLite dev / PostgreSQL prod)
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL is the primary/production database but is made optional for contributors, with SQLite as the zero-setup development fallback; the trade-off is lower onboarding cost in exchange for dialect differences that the ORM is expected to absorb.
nodes.norm_label: dual database strategy (sqlite dev / postgresql prod)

nodes.label: TensorFlow / PyTorch
nodes.rationale: Both frameworks are declared rather than one, which keeps model-format choice open per subsystem (detection vs recommendation) at the cost of a much heavier dependency footprint.

nodes.label: React.js Frontend
nodes.rationale: Frontend is a separate React SPA on port 3000 talking to the API on port 8000, keeping the ML/AI backend fully decoupled from the UI runtime.

nodes.label: ml_models/ (detection, recommender, training scripts)
nodes.rationale: Model weights and training scripts live outside backend/app so training code is never shipped with the serving application and models can be retrained independently of API releases.

nodes.label: Docker Deployment (split backend/frontend images)
nodes.rationale: Separate Dockerfile.backend and Dockerfile.frontend composed via docker-compose keep the heavy ML backend image independent of the lightweight Node/React build image.

nodes.label: Python Dependency Manifest
nodes.rationale: Organized into commented capability sections (web framework, database, auth, ML, CV, API clients, video, testing, logging, caching, background tasks, docs) and pinned with >= floors only, favouring easy upgrades over reproducible builds — there is no lockfile.

nodes.label: JWT Authentication & Password Hashing Stack
nodes.rationale: python-jose[cryptography] for JWT issuance/verification plus passlib[bcrypt] for password hashing — the conventional FastAPI auth pairing; python-multipart is required for form-encoded login and file/image upload endpoints.

nodes.label: sqlite3 listed as a PyPI requirement
nodes.rationale: Defect: sqlite3 is a Python standard-library module, not an installable distribution. The inline comment ('Built-in for development') acknowledges this, yet the line is left in the install list, so `pip install -r requirements.txt` will fail to resolve it. Duplicated entries (Pillow at lines 25/41, opencv-python at lines 28/46) show the manifest was assembled section-by-section without deduplication.
nodes.norm_label: sqlite3 listed as a pypi requirement

nodes.label: HuggingFace Transformers
nodes.rationale: Present in the manifest although the README tech-stack section never mentions it, suggesting planned local model inference beyond the two external generative APIs.

nodes.label: scikit-learn / pandas / numpy
nodes.rationale: Classical-ML stack, the plausible implementation substrate for the recommender rather than the deep-learning frameworks.

nodes.label: Celery Background Task Queue
nodes.rationale: Long-running generative calls (video and image synthesis) cannot fit inside an HTTP request cycle, so an out-of-band worker queue is required; flower is included for queue observability.

nodes.label: Redis Caching Layer
nodes.rationale: Serves double duty as a response cache for expensive third-party AI/nutrition API calls and as the natural Celery broker/result backend; redis-py-cluster anticipates a clustered deployment.

nodes.label: Async HTTP Clients for AI Services (requests / httpx / aiohttp)
nodes.rationale: Three overlapping HTTP clients are declared; async-capable clients (httpx, aiohttp) are needed so outbound generative-API calls do not block FastAPI's event loop, while requests covers sync/worker-side calls.
nodes.norm_label: async http clients for ai services (requests / httpx / aiohttp)

nodes.label: Spoonacular Recipe API client
nodes.rationale: External recipe/nutrition data is sourced from a third-party API rather than being fully self-hosted, complementing the local data/recipes datasets.

nodes.label: MoviePy Video Processing
nodes.rationale: Post-processing layer for generated footage (trimming, concatenation, overlays) applied after Google Flow returns raw video.

nodes.label: Test & Lint Toolchain (pytest, black, isort, flake8)
nodes.rationale: pytest-asyncio is included specifically because FastAPI route and async service tests are coroutine-based; dev tooling is mixed into the single runtime manifest rather than split into requirements-dev.txt.
nodes.norm_label: test & lint toolchain (pytest, black, isort, flake8)

nodes.label: Environment-based Configuration (dotenv / decouple / pydantic-settings)
nodes.rationale: Secrets and DATABASE_URL are injected via .env files so the same image runs against SQLite or PostgreSQL and against real AI provider keys without code changes.
